568.title: How am I using my soul?
568.hook: ask often: what am I using my soul for right now? (Meditations 5.11)
568.carry: what am I using it for
568.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes set reminders to ask the question of Meditations 5.11, 'what am I using my soul for right now?', several times a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: back to it, returning without disgust. Your line was a sponge and egg.

Your phone has a battery screen that shows exactly where the power went. Maps, twelve percent. Messages, twenty. That one game, a slightly embarrassing forty. Nobody has a screen like that for attention, or for the inner life. If you did, what would today's breakdown say? Marcus Aurelius didn't have the screen, but he had the question, and he wrote it down as a short, sharp check.
screen: `THE BATTERY SCREEN.` → `WHERE DID THE POWER GO?` → `HOW AM I USING MY SOUL?`

segments.voice: What am I using my soul for right now? Marcus writes this in book five, entry eleven, and says to ask it on every occasion. Not once a year at a retreat. Now, and now again. Then he sharpens it: what is going on in the part of me they call the ruling part? The Stoics' word was hegemonikon, the steering center of a person, where judgments and choices happen. He wants to check who's at the wheel. And then the striking part. Whose soul do I have right now? A child's? A teenager's? A tyrant's? A farm animal's? A wild beast's? It's almost funny, and it's very honest. On some days a person might cycle through several: the child who wants it now, the tyrant who wants it done my way, the grazing animal scrolling for the next bite, the wild animal in traffic. The question isn't a test you pass. It's a mirror you keep glancing at. Each time you ask, you get a little gap: you notice the tyrant, and the noticing can loosen his grip. Asked often enough, it becomes a habit of returning, which was yesterday's whole lesson. You don't have to fix the answer. Just hear it.

569.title: The river of being
569.hook: think how fast things pass by, like a river (Meditations 5.23)
569.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes watch moving water and recall Meditations 5.23, letting both worries and successes be seen as part of a constant flow.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hegemonikon, the ruling part. Your line was what am I using it for.

A river has a name on the map. From a bridge it looks like one steady thing, the same river it was last year. But not one drop under the bridge now was there a minute ago. The river is real, and it's also never the same twice. Centuries before Marcus Aurelius, a Greek thinker named Heraclitus made that observation famous. Marcus picked it up and turned it on everything, including himself.
screen: `A RIVER FROM A BRIDGE.` → `NOT ONE DROP IS THE SAME.` → `THE RIVER OF BEING.`

segments.voice: Think often, Marcus writes in book five, entry twenty-three, how fast the things that are, and the things coming to be, are carried past and out of sight. Not once: a habit of seeing. Being itself, he says, is like a river in continual flow. Its activities keep changing, its causes shift in countless ways, and almost nothing stands still. Heraclitus, as Plato reports him, said you could not step into the same river twice. Marcus lays that river over the whole world: cities, bodies, moods, reputations, problems. And close beside us, he says, is the boundless gulf of past and future, into which everything vanishes. We met that gulf near the end of book four; here it's the sea the river runs into. Then the practical turn. Isn't it foolish, he asks, to be puffed up, or tormented, or upset by these things, as if any of them would trouble us for long? A worry flooding in today is water, already moving. A flush of pride is water too. The river picture works in both directions. It softens the hard thing, because it will pass. And it keeps the good thing light, so you enjoy it without clutching. You don't have to stop the river. You only have to stop pretending it's a lake.

570.title: Bad breath
570.hook: angry at someone's bad breath? what can he do, it's his mouth (Meditations 5.28)
570.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes recall Meditations 5.28 with small irritations: either it can't be helped, so let it go, or it can, so mention it kindly.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Heraclitus, and the river that never stays the same. Your line was the river.

Of all the things you might expect in a Roman emperor's private notebook, a note about body odor is near the bottom of the list. And yet there it is, in book five, entry twenty-eight. He doesn't say whether he had anyone in mind. But the picture is vivid: sweaty armpits, bad breath, and someone close enough to notice, getting irritated. He uses it to think something through, and it's very practical.
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S NOTEBOOK.` → `A NOTE ABOUT BODY ODOR.` → `BAD BREATH.`

segments.voice: Are you angry with someone whose armpits smell, Marcus asks himself, or whose breath is bad? What good will that do you? He has the mouth he has, and the armpits he has. A smell like that has to come from things like that. A lot of small annoyances work the same way. The loud chewer. The slow walker. The coworker who says actually before every sentence. These come out of who they are and how they're made, not out of a plan to bother you. Then Marcus imagines an objection: but the man has reason, you'll say; he could notice and fix it. Fine, Marcus replies. You have reason too. So use your reasoning to stir up his. Show him. Tell him, kindly. If he listens, you'll have cured it, and there's no need for anger. And no theatrics either, he adds: not the tragic actor, and not the opposite extreme. Just calm, plain dealing. So every small annoyance comes down to two honest options. Either it isn't theirs to change, and anger is pointless. Or it is, and a kind word works better than anger does. Either way, anger isn't needed. And there's something warm under the joke: Marcus's answer is not to avoid the man, but to help him.

571.title: Soon ashes
571.hook: soon you'll be ashes; meanwhile, revere and do good (Meditations 5.33)
571.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes use the plain reminder of Meditations 5.33, 'soon ashes', to clear away small quarrels and do one good act right away.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bad breath: he has the mouth he has. Your line was it's his mouth.

Ashes is a word people tend to keep at a distance, for funerals and a few solemn days a year. Marcus Aurelius kept it closer. In book five, entry thirty-three, he writes it to himself very plainly: you'll be ashes soon. Then, in the same breath, he asks what a person should do with the time in between. His answer is short, and it isn't gloomy at all. It's a to-do list.
screen: `WE KEEP THE WORD AT A DISTANCE.` → `MARCUS KEPT IT CLOSE.` → `SOON ASHES.`

segments.voice: Soon, very soon, Marcus writes, you'll be ashes, or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name. And a name is only a sound and an echo. Then he looks at what people spend their lives fighting over. The things most prized in life, he says, are empty and small: puppies snapping at each other, children quarreling, laughing, and then crying a minute later. He borrows a phrase from the Greek poet Hesiod, about virtues fleeing the wide earth for Olympus, and applies it to faithfulness, modesty, justice and truth. A wry picture of a world that often forgets what matters. So what holds him here, he asks, since the things we sense are always changing and our senses are easily fooled? His answer: wait calmly for the end, whatever it turns out to be. And meanwhile, what's enough? To revere the gods and speak well of them. To do good to people. To bear with them, and to hold back. And to remember that whatever lies outside your own small flesh and breath is not yours and not up to you. Marcus doesn't use ashes to stop himself living. He uses it to clear the desk. The squabbles drop off. What's left fits on a card: reverence, kindness, patience, restraint. For him, reverence meant the gods of Stoic belief; readers on many paths keep that part in their own words, or in none. The rest is open to anyone: do good, now, while there's a now.

572.title: The child's top
572.hook: like an old man keeping a child's toy, comfort others without being swept away (Meditations 5.36)
572.howItsDone: People who practice Stoic ethics often describe comforting others warmly while keeping their own judgment about what is truly harmful, rather than either lecturing or catching the panic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: soon ashes, and the job Marcus gives the time in between. Your line was meanwhile, do good.

A four-year-old drops an ice cream cone on the sidewalk. The wail is total. The world has ended. Two grown-ups are standing there. One says, it's only ice cream, stop crying. The other kneels down, says, oh no, your cone, and holds the child until the storm passes. Neither of them thinks the cone was a tragedy. Only one of them was any comfort. Near the end of book five, Marcus Aurelius has a picture for the second grown-up: an old man and a child's spinning top.
screen: `THE DROPPED CONE.` → `TWO GROWN-UPS.` → `AN OLD MAN AND A TOP.`

segments.voice: Marcus believes most of what people grieve over isn't truly harmful: money, a post, a reputation. Only acting badly harms the self. That could make a Stoic cold. Someone loses their job, and the Stoic says, that's an indifferent, you're fine. Marcus doesn't want that. In book five, entry thirty-six, he says: don't be carried away by how things look. Help people as far as you can and as each case deserves, even when what they've lost is one of those indifferent things. But don't imagine the loss is a real harm to them; that's a bad habit of mind. Then the picture: be like the old man who, when he was leaving, asked for his foster child's top back, remembering all along that it was a top. He takes the toy seriously because the child does. He just doesn't forget what it is. An honest note: the Greek here is compressed, and the end of this section is partly damaged in the manuscripts. Translators fill the gaps in different ways, and scholars still argue about exactly what the old man is doing. The core is clear enough: kindness on the outside, clarity on the inside. The old man never lies to the child, and he doesn't lecture. He meets the child where the child is, and keeps his own head. That's a skill most of us need at a hospital bedside, a breakup, a lost game. Be warm with the sorrow. Stay clear about the size of things, privately.

573.title: Cold or warm
573.hook: whether you're cold or warm, sleepy or rested, do your duty (Meditations 6.2)
573.carry: nobody claps, the work is good anyway
573.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use 'cold or warm' as a private reminder when they're tired or unappreciated, to do the task in front of them as well as they would on a good day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus's old man, who took a toy seriously for a child's sake. Your line was honest comfort.

Three in the morning. The baby is crying again, and it's your turn. Or the alarm goes off for the early shift and the room is freezing. Or you promised to help a friend move, and you slept four hours. It's easy to keep a list of conditions for doing a thing well: warm, rested, appreciated, in the mood. Book six of the Meditations opens, and its second entry crosses that whole list out.
screen: `THREE A.M., YOUR TURN.` → `THE LIST OF CONDITIONS.` → `BOOK SIX OPENS.`

segments.voice: In George Long's translation, Meditations six, two begins: "Let it make no difference to thee whether thou art cold or warm, if thou art doing thy duty." Then Marcus keeps going, pair by pair. Drowsy or rested. Spoken badly of or praised. Even dying or doing something else. Each pair is a condition we use as an excuse. I'll be patient when I've slept. I'll be generous when people notice. Marcus treats them all as weather: real, uncomfortable, and not in charge. Then the surprise at the end. He says dying is one of the acts of life too, and in that act, as in any other, it's enough to do well the thing in hand. He doesn't make death a special exam. It's one more task, done as well as you can on the day it comes. What he isn't saying: ignore your body, or never rest. Elsewhere he admits that staying under the covers feels more pleasant. The point is narrower. When the duty is actually yours, right now, the shivering isn't a reason to do it badly. And there's a quiet dignity in work done well while tired. A nurse at the end of a double shift. A parent at three in the morning. Nobody claps. The work is good anyway.

segments.voice: Yesterday: cold or warm, the duty that doesn't wait for perfect conditions. Your line was nobody claps, the work is good anyway. And today the week closes.

Someone cuts you off in traffic, then honks at you. A coworker takes credit in the meeting. A relative says the cutting thing at dinner, the one they always say. And instantly, the reply is ready: sharper, faster, a little crueler, because they started it. It can feel like justice. Marcus Aurelius was an emperor. He could have answered almost any insult with real force. In book six he writes himself one short sentence about revenge.
screen: `THE REPLY IS ALREADY LOADED.` → `AN EMPEROR'S OPTIONS.` → `ONE SENTENCE ON REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Meditations six, six, in George Long's translation: "The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer." He doesn't say there's no such thing as being wronged. Someone did wrong. The question is what you do next. When someone is rude and you're rude back, two people have now been rude, and one of them is you. Their behavior has reached inside you and rearranged you. For a Stoic, that's the only real damage they could do. Your money, your reputation, those are outside. Your character is the one thing that's yours, and mirroring them hands it over. Why call it revenge? Marcus could have said forgive, or rise above it. Instead he keeps the word revenge, and there's something a little sly in that. He lets the hurt part of you have its wish to win, then changes what winning means. The wrongdoer wanted you smaller. You stay the size you were. Now look back at this week. How am I using my soul. Heraclitus. Bad breath, where someone's mouth is just their mouth. Soon ashes, and meanwhile, do good. The child's top. Cold or warm. And now this. Nearly every one of those lines is about the same small room: the space between what happens to you and what you become because of it. Marcus keeps returning to that room, because it's the one place nobody else can enter without your permission.
screen: `AVENGE YOURSELF: DON'T BECOME THEM.` · `MIRRORING HANDS THEM YOUR CHARACTER.` · `HE KEEPS THE WORD REVENGE.` · `THIS WEEK: THE SAME SMALL ROOM.` · then, large: `NOT LIKE THEM.`

segments.voice: Recall one recent moment when someone was rude or unfair to you, and notice where the comeback sits in your body: jaw, chest, hands. Now replay the scene with you answering in your own voice instead of theirs, calm, plain, maybe silent. Not weak; just not like them.
George Long, whose translation gives Marcus's line: the best way of avenging yourself is not to become like the one who wronged you. Today's word.
Your line: not like them. You stay the size you were. Week's end; see you tomorrow.
